questions.title: N+1 Query Problem in Spring Data JPA
questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem in JPA/Hibernate and how do you fix it?
questions.direct_answer: N+1 happens when JPA fires **1 query to load N parent entities**, then fires **N more queries to load each parent's lazy association** — loading 100 orders and touching each order's customer triggers **101 SQL statements** instead of 1 or 2. Three fixes: **`JOIN FETCH`** in JPQL eagerly joins the association in the same query but **breaks pagination with collections** (Hibernate paginates in memory, logs `HHH90003004`); **`@EntityGraph`** declares the same eager fetch per-method and is Spring Data's idiomatic alternative; **`@BatchSize`** on the association reduces N+1 to `N/batchSize + 1` using `WHERE id IN (?,?,...)` and works with pagination. Diagnose with `spring.jpa.show-sql=true`, assert query counts in integration tests via Hibernate Statistics, and prefer **DTO projections** for read-heavy endpoints.

sections.title: The Query That Runs Once Should Run Once — Not 101 Times
sections.content:
The N+1 problem is the most common performance issue in JPA applications. You write one query to load N entities, then Hibernate fires N additional queries to load each entity's lazy association — one per entity. Loading 100 orders with their customers generates **101 SQL statements** instead of 1 or 2.

The problem is **invisible in development**. With 5 test orders, 6 queries take milliseconds. In production with 1,000 orders, 1,001 queries take seconds. **The fix is always to fetch the association in the original query** rather than letting Hibernate load them one at a time.

Developers who know only `JOIN FETCH` miss important trade-offs.
- **`JOIN FETCH` cannot be used with pagination on collections** (Hibernate fetches all rows and paginates in memory with a warning). `@EntityGraph` is the Spring Data-friendly alternative. `@BatchSize` reduces N+1 to N/batch+1 without changing queries.
- Each fix has a different use case.

sections.title: N+1 Explosion vs JOIN FETCH Solution
sections.content: Visual contrast: 101 round trips for the lazy path, 1 round trip with `JOIN FETCH` (or 2 with `@BatchSize`).
sections.mermaid:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Bad["N+1 lazy access (101 queries)"]
        b1["orderRepo.findAll() -> 1 SELECT order"] --> b2["100 orders returned"]
        b2 --> b3["forEach: order.getCustomer().getName()"]
        b3 --> b4["Hibernate fires SELECT customer WHERE id = ?"]
        b4 --> b5["...repeats 100 times"]
        b5 --> b6["Total: 1 + 100 = 101 SQL round trips"]
    end

    subgraph GoodFetch["JOIN FETCH (1 query)"]
        g1["SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer"] --> g2["Single SQL with INNER JOIN"]
        g2 --> g3["100 orders + 100 customers in 1 round trip"]
        g3 --> g4["Caveat: collections + Pageable -> in-memory paginate (HHH90003004)"]
    end

    subgraph GoodBatch["@BatchSize (N/batch + 1 queries)"]
        bt1["@BatchSize(50) on customer"] --> bt2["SELECT order page (1 query)"]
        bt2 --> bt3["Lazy access triggers WHERE id IN (?,?,...50)"]
        bt3 --> bt4["100 customers in 2 batched queries"]
        bt4 --> bt5["Pagination compatible"]
    end

    Bad -.fix.-> GoodFetch
    Bad -.fix.-> GoodBatch

sections.title: Diagnosing N+1 — SQL Logging and the Hibernate Statistics API
sections.content:
**Make the queries visible:**
- `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` for development.
- `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG` for more control.
- `logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE` to see bind values.
- Count SELECT statements per API call — repeated query patterns with different bind values = N+1.

**Hibernate Statistics API for production:**
- Enable: `spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true`.
- Access via `sessionFactory.getStatistics().getQueryExecutionCount()` and `getPrepareStatementCount()`.
- Detect N+1 in integration tests by asserting query counts.

**Tooling:**
- `datasource-proxy` wraps the DataSource and logs every query with stack traces — finds which code path triggers extra queries.
- `p6spy` is a similar option.
- Production: expose Hibernate metrics through Micrometer; alert on anomaly spikes.

sections.title: Three Fixes and When Each One Fits
sections.content:
**`JOIN FETCH` in JPQL:**
- Loads association in the same query using SQL JOIN.
- `SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer` -> one query, one JOIN.
- **Trade-off**: breaks pagination on collections — `firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch` warning, in-memory paginate.
- Best for single-row detail views or `@ManyToOne` only.

**`@EntityGraph`:**
- Spring Data's declarative alternative.
- `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer")` on a repository method.
- Generates LEFT JOIN — same SQL as `JOIN FETCH` but no JPQL needed.
- Same pagination caveat for collections.

**`@BatchSize` on the association:**
- `@BatchSize(size = 25)` on the field.
- Hibernate batches lazy loads: `WHERE id IN (?,?,...)`.
- N+1 becomes `N/25 + 1` — for N=100, 4 queries instead of 100.
- **Works with pagination** because Hibernate batches lazily after the paginated query.
- Best when JOIN FETCH would break pagination.
- Optimal batch size 10-50.

**`@Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT)`:**
- When any item's collection is accessed, Hibernate loads all collections for the entire result set using `WHERE order_id IN (SELECT id FROM order WHERE ...)`.
- One extra query per relationship regardless of result set size.
- Ideal when you consistently need the association for all loaded parents.

sections.title: Decision Matrix — JOIN FETCH vs @EntityGraph vs @BatchSize vs DTO
sections.content:
Pick based on whether the query paginates, how many collections you need, and whether you return entities or DTOs.

| Approach | Syntax | SQL generated | Pagination compatible | Multiple collections | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **JOIN FETCH** | JPQL `SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items` | Single query with INNER/LEFT JOIN | No — collections break it | No — Cartesian product | Single-valued `@ManyToOne`, non-paginated queries |
| **@EntityGraph** | `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items"})` | Single query with LEFT JOIN FETCH | No — same caveat for collections | No — Cartesian product | Reusable, declarative; avoids JPQL |
| **@BatchSize** | `@BatchSize(size = 50)` on field | `WHERE id IN (...)` batches; `N/batch + 1` queries | Yes | Yes — each collection batched independently | Paginated queries, mixed needs |
| **@Fetch(SUBSELECT)** | `@Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT)` | One subquery per association | Yes | Yes | All parents always need all children |
| **DTO projection** | `SELECT new com.x.OrderDTO(...)` | Single query, no entities | Yes | Yes — no Cartesian product | Read-heavy list views, exports |

**Decision shortcut:**
- One parent + children for a detail view -> `JOIN FETCH` or `@EntityGraph`.
- A page of parents -> `@BatchSize` on the collection + `Pageable`.
- A list for display (no edits) -> DTO projection.
- Multiple collections on one parent -> separate queries combined into a DTO.

**The HHH90003004 warning is the tell.** `firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory` -> Hibernate has loaded the entire unpaginated result set and paginated in Java. Latent OOM. Switch to `@BatchSize` or DTO.

sections.title: Runnable Example — Triggering, Measuring, and Fixing an N+1
Pitfalls, Edge Cases, and a Production Checklist
sections.content:
**When fixes help:**
- `JOIN FETCH` / `@EntityGraph` collapse N+1 to a single query for non-paginated reads.
- `@BatchSize` works with pagination and requires no query changes.
- DTO projections eliminate N+1 by skipping entity loading altogether.

**When fixes hurt (Cartesian product trap):**
- Two `@OneToMany` collections in one `JOIN FETCH` (e.g., `items` and `payments`).
- Order with 20 items and 5 payments returns 100 rows.
- Hibernate deduplicates in memory but transferred 5x bytes over the wire.
- Always fetch collections in **separate queries** or with `@BatchSize`.

**Watch for:**
- **`DISTINCT` is a Hibernate-specific hint** — `SELECT DISTINCT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items` deduplicates parents in memory; use `passDistinctThrough = false` query hint to suppress SQL `DISTINCT`.
- **`Set` vs `List`** — `Set` deduplicates automatically (no DISTINCT) but requires `equals/hashCode` consistency; using a generated ID in equals breaks the Set when entities are unsaved.
- **`findAll()` is never acceptable in production** — always combine with `Pageable` or filter.
- **`FetchType.EAGER` on associations is a trap** — triggers on every query whether you need the association or not; always LAZY by default, opt-in per query.
- **`spring.jpa.open-in-view=true` is the Spring Boot default** — keeps session open across view render; hides N+1 because lazy loads succeed silently in the controller. **Disable it.** Lazy access outside a transaction then throws `LazyInitializationException` — a loud error instead of a silent performance bug.

**Production checklist:**
- `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false`
- All `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToMany` set to `fetch = FetchType.LAZY`
- Every `JOIN FETCH` with collections checked for pagination usage
- `@BatchSize` on collections accessed in paginated queries
- DTO projections for list views; entities only for commands/edits
- Query count assertions in integration tests (HibernateStatistics)
- Production monitoring: `hibernate.query.count` metric with anomaly alerts
- `datasource-proxy` or p6spy in dev to log every SQL with stack trace
- Never use `findAll()` without `Pageable`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **N+1 = 1 query for N parents + N queries for the lazy association** — 100 orders + customers = 101 queries.
- **`JOIN FETCH`** — JPQL keyword; one query with JOIN; breaks pagination on collections.
- **`@EntityGraph`** — Spring Data declarative; same SQL, same pagination caveat for collections.
- **`@BatchSize`** — reduces N+1 to `N/batch + 1`; works with pagination.
- **DTO projection** — `SELECT new ...` returns plain objects; no proxies, no lazy access, no N+1 possible.
- **`spring.jpa.show-sql=true` + query count test** — make N+1 visible and prevent regressions.
- **`spring.jpa.open-in-view=false`** mandatory for REST APIs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
N+1 is the most common JPA performance bug. Loading a collection of entities and then accessing a lazy association on each — one query for the parents, one query per parent for the association.

**The classic example:**
- `List<Order> orders = orderRepo.findAll()` — 1 query, 100 orders
- `orders.forEach(o -> o.getItems().size())` — 100 additional queries
- Total: 101 SQL queries to do what one JOIN could accomplish

**Fix 1 — `JOIN FETCH` in JPQL:**
- `@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items WHERE o.status = :status")`
- One SQL with a JOIN
- Limitation: cannot combine `JOIN FETCH` with `Pageable` on a collection — in-memory pagination warning

**Fix 2 — `@EntityGraph`:**
- `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items"})` on the repository method
- Spring translates to LEFT JOIN FETCH; same caveat with collection pagination

**Fix 3 — `@BatchSize`:**
- `@BatchSize(size = 25)` on the collection field
- Hibernate batches lazy loads: instead of 100 queries, 4 `WHERE id IN (...)` queries
- Easiest to add, fully compatible with pagination

**Fix 4 — DTO projection:**
- `SELECT new com.x.OrderDto(...)` returns plain objects
- No entities, no proxies, no possibility of N+1

questions.title: Solving N+1 with @EntityGraph
questions.question: How do you use @EntityGraph in Spring Data JPA to solve N+1 without writing JPQL JOIN FETCH queries?
questions.direct_answer: **`@EntityGraph`** is Spring Data's declarative answer to N+1: annotate a repository method with `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"customer", "items"})` and Hibernate generates a **LEFT JOIN FETCH** for those attributes only for that query, leaving the entity's default `FetchType.LAZY` intact for every other query. It is cleaner than writing JPQL `JOIN FETCH` by hand, composes with derived queries (no `@Query` needed), and accepts both ad-hoc `attributePaths` and reusable **`@NamedEntityGraph`** declarations on the entity. The two graph types — **`FETCH`** (only graph attributes are eager, all others LAZY) and **`LOAD`** (graph attributes eager, others follow entity defaults) — let you override EAGER-mapped associations back to LAZY per query. Same pagination caveat as `JOIN FETCH`: collection graphs + `Pageable` trigger in-memory pagination (HHH90003004). For paginated list views, use **`@BatchSize`**.

sections.title: @EntityGraph Is Spring Data's Declarative Alternative to JOIN FETCH — With the Same Pagination Trap
sections.content:
Writing `JOIN FETCH` JPQL queries for every repository method gets repetitive. **`@EntityGraph` lets you declare which associations to fetch eagerly** on a per-query basis, directly on Spring Data repository method signatures, without writing JPQL.

Under the hood, `@EntityGraph` generates a LEFT JOIN — the same SQL as `JOIN FETCH`. This means it carries the **same pagination caveat**: combining `@EntityGraph` with `Pageable` on a collection association causes Hibernate to load all rows into memory and paginate in Java, logging the HHH90003004 warning.

Two graph types: **FETCH** (attributes in graph eager, all others follow default fetch type) and **LOAD** (attributes in graph eager, all others follow **entity-level** fetch type — EAGER stays EAGER). The distinction matters when you want `@EntityGraph` to override EAGER associations to LAZY — only **FETCH** does that.

sections.title: Ad-hoc vs Named EntityGraphs — When Reuse Justifies the Annotation
sections.content:
**Ad-hoc `attributePaths` on the repository method:**
- Cleanest for simple cases.
- No entity annotation needed.

```java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"customer", "items"})
    List<Order> findByStatus(String status);
}
```

- Tells Hibernate to LEFT JOIN `customer` and `items`.
- Same repository can have another method without `@EntityGraph` that loads orders lazily — each method controls its own fetch strategy.

**`@NamedEntityGraph` on the entity:**
- Define graph once on the entity, reference by name in repositories.
- Avoids duplicating `attributePaths` across multiple methods.
- Best for graphs reused across multiple repositories or services.

**For paginated queries with collections:**
- Avoid `@EntityGraph` entirely.
- Use `@BatchSize` on the association.
- Or split: load parent IDs with pagination first, then load full entities with `@EntityGraph` using the ID list.

sections.title: EntityGraph Limitations — When It Does Not Save You
sections.content:
**Multiple `@OneToMany` collections in one EntityGraph -> Cartesian product:**
- Same problem as multiple `JOIN FETCH`es.
- Order with 20 items and 5 payments -> 100-row result set, deduplicated by Hibernate.
- Inefficient at scale.
- Fix: load each collection in **separate queries** or use `@BatchSize`.

**`@EntityGraph` + paginated query with collections:**
- Triggers `HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory`.
- Hibernate loads all rows (ignoring page size), paginates in memory.
- Latent OOM.
- Fix: paginate parent IDs (no JOIN), then fetch with `@EntityGraph` using `findByIdIn(ids)`.

**Native queries:**
- `@EntityGraph` is JPQL-only.
- Native SQL must use explicit JOINs and projections.

**`@BatchSize` after pagination:**
- Paginate the parents (works correctly with no JOIN).
- Let `@BatchSize` load collections in batches after pagination is applied.
- COUNT and data queries only touch parent table — pagination works correctly.

sections.title: FETCH vs LOAD Graph Types — Which Overrides Your Entity Mapping
sections.content:
The two `EntityGraph.EntityGraphType` values behave very differently when the entity has `FetchType.EAGER` declarations.

| Scenario | Entity mapping | Graph type | Attribute in graph | Attribute NOT in graph |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FETCH (default)** | `@ManyToOne(fetch = EAGER) Customer customer` | FETCH | Eager | **LAZY** (overrides entity default) |
| **FETCH (default)** | `@OneToMany(fetch = LAZY) List<Item> items` | FETCH | Eager | LAZY |
| **LOAD** | `@ManyToOne(fetch = EAGER) Customer customer` | LOAD | Eager | **Still EAGER** (entity default wins) |
| **LOAD** | `@OneToMany(fetch = LAZY) List<Item> items` | LOAD | Eager | LAZY |

**Practical implication:**
- **FETCH** is safer and stricter — guarantees attributes not in the graph are LAZY.
- **LOAD** respects entity's original mapping for unlisted attributes — useful if you explicitly want EAGER associations to stay EAGER.

```java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items"}, type = EntityGraph.EntityGraphType.FETCH)
List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);
```

**Rule of thumb:** default to `FETCH` so queries are self-describing — reading the method tells you exactly which associations are loaded.

sections.title: Limitations and Patterns for Multi-Collection Fetches
sections.content:
**When `@EntityGraph` helps:**
- Loading a single entity by ID for a detail page.
- Non-paginated list queries with one collection.
- Replacing repetitive `JOIN FETCH` JPQL with a declarative annotation.
- Reusable named graphs for cross-repository consistency.

**When `@EntityGraph` hurts:**
- Pagination + collection -> in-memory pagination, latent OOM.
- Multiple `@OneToMany` -> Cartesian product blowup.
- Native queries -> not supported.
- Deep graphs (3+ levels) -> result set explosion.

**Three patterns for loading multiple collections:**

1. **Separate service calls, join in memory.** Load orders with `items`, then load orders with `payments`, merge by ID. Two small queries beat one giant JOIN.

2. **ID-first pagination.** Step 1: page parent IDs with a filter query (no collections). Step 2: load full entities with `@EntityGraph` using `findByIdIn(pageIds)` — no pagination, no HHH90003004.

3. **DTO projection with `SIZE()` or aggregate subquery.** For list views needing only counts, `SELECT new OrderSummary(o.id, SIZE(o.items), SIZE(o.payments))` is one query, one row per order, no Cartesian.

**Watch for:**
- Always profile generated SQL with `spring.jpa.show-sql=true` when combining `@EntityGraph` + `Pageable`.
- Subgraphs let you declare deep graphs (`@NamedSubgraph`).
- Use `jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph` or `jakarta.persistence.loadgraph` query hints for dynamic graphs built at runtime.

sections.title: Three Production-Grade Patterns Using @EntityGraph
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@EntityGraph` = per-query eager fetching** — no entity mapping changes; Hibernate generates LEFT JOIN FETCH.
- **Named vs ad-hoc** — `@NamedEntityGraph` on entity for reuse; `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {...})` on method for one-offs.
- **Same pagination caveat as `JOIN FETCH`** — collection graph + `Pageable` -> in-memory pagination warning.
- **Cartesian product on multi-collection graphs** — split into separate queries or use `@BatchSize`.
- **`FETCH` vs `LOAD`** — FETCH overrides EAGER to LAZY for unlisted; LOAD keeps entity defaults.
- **Dynamic graphs** — build `EntityGraph` at runtime via `EntityManager.createEntityGraph()`.
- **ID-first pagination** is the canonical fix for paginated list views with collections.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@EntityGraph` solves N+1 by telling Hibernate which associations to fetch eagerly for a specific query, without changing the entity's default fetch strategy. It is the clean solution when `JOIN FETCH` breaks pagination.

**How it works:**
- Declare an ad-hoc graph on the repository method: `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items", "items.product"})`
- Hibernate translates this to LEFT JOIN FETCH on those paths for that query only
- The entity's `@OneToMany(fetch = LAZY)` stays LAZY for all other queries

**Named vs ad-hoc graphs:**
- Named: `@NamedEntityGraph(name = "Order.withItems", attributeNodes = @NamedAttributeNode("items"))` on the entity class; reference by name
- Ad-hoc: `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items"})` directly on the repository method — preferred for most cases

**Pagination compatibility:**
- `JOIN FETCH` + `Pageable` on a collection triggers HHH90003004 warning and in-memory pagination — dangerous on large datasets
- `@EntityGraph` carries the same caveat — for paginated collections, paginate IDs first or use `@BatchSize`

**Over-fetching trap:**
- Fetching multiple `@OneToMany` associations in one graph produces a Cartesian product
- Prefer separate queries or DTO projections when you need data from multiple collection associations
